wave: CORRECTNESS -- two real defects in the Rust extractor's STATE dimension: (1) a field used as a mutating method call's receiver (`self.list.push(x)`) was confidently claimed as a Read and NEVER as a Write, misrepresenting a real mutation -- a fabricated-in-effect claim, not merely a coverage gap, violating this exact module's own documented 'never fabricate a spurious Read of a place computation' doctrine; (2) a compound-assignment through an index into a field (`self.data[i] += 1`) lost its Write entirely, falling back to a plain Read, contradicting the module's own explicitly documented and tested read-modify-write guarantee for compound assignment.
wave_title: Twenty-eighth generation this cycle. Continuing the standing correctness priority. priority_classification: correctness -- Finding 1 is a fabricated-claim-class defect (worse than a mere gap: a definite, wrong Read claim for an operation that may be a real Write), reachable from extremely common Rust code (any `&mut self` method call on a field, e.g. `.push`/`.insert`/`.remove`/`.clear`/`.sort` on a Vec field). Finding 2 is a real under-approximation against an explicitly documented and tested invariant (compound assignment is always read-modify-write), reachable whenever a compound-assign target is an indexed field.
gap_discovered_by: A background Explore subagent survey, scoped to EFFECT/STATE/CONCURRENCY/PERSISTENCE classification logic after this session's earlier CFG/dataflow and CALL fixes. Independently re-verified before acting: read state.rs's real Expr::MethodCall and Expr::Binary compound-assign arms directly, read the module's own doc comment (which explicitly states the exact 'never fabricate a spurious Read of an intermediate place' principle that Finding 1 violates), and confirmed via grep/read that OWNERSHIP already has a directly analogous, already-battle-tested precedent for the identical epistemic gap (a method-call receiver is never treated as a move-or-copy site, since whether it takes &self or &mut self cannot be told from the call site alone).
key_finding: Finding 1: state.rs's Expr::MethodCall arm walked the receiver via the generic recursive walk_expr, which -- when the receiver is a resolvable self.field chain -- hits the ordinary Expr::Field arm and unconditionally emits StateAccessKind::Read, with no special-casing for 'this field is being taken as a call receiver.' A field mutated by ANY standard &mut self method (.push/.insert/.remove/.clear/.sort/.extend/...) therefore produces only a Read event and never a Write, for every real call site of this shape. Finding 2: the compound-assign special case in the Expr::Binary arm only recognized binary.left as directly Expr::Field; an Expr::Index whose own base resolves to a self field (self.data[i] += 1) fell through to a generic walk that emits a plain Read via the Index arm's own field-base handling, with no Write at all -- contradicting the module's own explicit, tested RMW guarantee for compound assignment, which only actually held for a bare field target.
verification_before_acting: Read state.rs's real, unfixed Expr::MethodCall arm directly, confirming it delegates to the generic Field-Read-emitting arm with no receiver-specific handling.

Read state.rs's real, unfixed Expr::Binary compound-assign arm directly, confirming it only special-cases a literal Expr::Field left-hand side, falling through generically (and losing the Write) for an Expr::Index target.

Read state.rs's own module doc comment directly, confirming its own stated principle ('evaluating an intermediate place... is a pure place computation, never a value read... fabricating a spurious Read... would misrepresent Rust's own place-expression semantics') applies identically to a method-call receiver, even though the doc's own text only explicitly discusses intermediate CHAIN links.

Read adapter/src/semantic/rust/ownership.rs's own module doc comment directly, confirming it already establishes the exact same 'method call receiver's mutability cannot be told without type resolution' reasoning as settled precedent in this codebase, giving Finding 1's fix a direct, already-battle-tested design template rather than inventing a new policy.
Grepped tests.rs for any existing test using a field as a method-call receiver or a compound-assign-through-index target before writing new fixtures -- confirmed neither shape was covered.

design_decisions.question: For a method-call receiver field, emit a Write (since the common case IS mutation), a Read (the current, wrong behavior), or nothing?
design_decisions.decision: Emit nothing. The extractor has no type information to distinguish &self from &mut self method calls -- guessing Write would be equally fabricated for the common read-only case (.len(), .get(), .iter(), .clone()), and the current Read claim is provably wrong for the common mutating case. Mirrors OWNERSHIP's own already-established, already-tested precedent for the identical gap: stay silent rather than guess, consistent with this codebase's 'never fabricate compiler-resolved semantics' doctrine applied throughout every extraction dimension.

design_decisions.question: For the indexed compound-assign case, is emitting both Read and Write actually safe (not a guess), unlike the method-call case?
design_decisions.decision: Yes -- this is a fundamentally different epistemic situation. Compound assignment is READ-MODIFY-WRITE by Rust's own static grammar, unconditionally, regardless of what type is being indexed (no method-dispatch ambiguity is involved at all). The only question was whether the walker's shape-matching correctly recognized an Index-wrapped field target, not whether the RMW claim itself needed type resolution -- so extending the existing, already-correct RMW emission to also handle this shape is safe, not a new guess.
